Good question to settle before anything else. A sample space lists all possible outcomes of an experiment: every result that could happen, each written exactly once, with nothing left out and nothing counted twice. For coins, that means every sequence of heads and tails the flips could produce. An event is a set of outcomes picked from that list, the particular results you care about, such as every sequence with at least one head. The two ideas work together: the sample space is the complete list, and an event is a selection from it. That is why problems give you two counts, the size of the event and the size of the whole list, and why the order of work is always the same: write the full list first, then pick out the outcomes the event wants. Knowing that fact changes what counts: every outcome that contradicts the condition is set aside, and only the outcomes that agree with it stay in play. Those remaining outcomes are the condition group.
